readerTitle: Why good subscriptions still get cancelled
caseNote: 가상 사례 (개인 가계부 정리, 명상 앱, 공장용 필터 정기배송) + 널리 관찰되는 현상(구독 피로)에 대한 일반적 설명 · 구체 통계는 쓰지 않음
insight: 구독은 혼자 평가받지 않는다. 고객은 정리하는 순간 모든 정기 결제를 한 줄로 세우고 맨 아래부터 자른다. 내 진짜 경쟁자는 같은 명세서에 찍힌 다른 구독들이다.
misconception: 고객이 만족하고 가격이 싸면 구독은 알아서 계속 유지된다. 해지는 제품이 나쁘다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: 'Subscription fatigue'는 소비자 구독 증가와 함께 경영·언론에서 널리 쓰이는 일반 개념이며, 이 레슨은 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않음
모든 인물, 회사, 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 레슨 안의 수치(정기 결제 11건, 월 $9 앱 등)는 모두 가상입니다. 구독 지출 과소추정 등 외부 설문 수치는 출처 신뢰도 문제로 넣지 않았습니다. 추가하려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.
6번 카드의 '기업 재무팀이 정기 계약을 주기적으로 점검한다'는 일반적 관행 서술입니다. 특정 비율이나 통계로 바꾸지 마세요.
7번 카드에서 해지를 어렵게 만드는 관행의 법적 규제는 국가별로 달라 언급하지 않았습니다(가이드상 법률 조언 범위 밖).

cards.title: Why good subscriptions still get cancelled
body: Sunday night. Maya opens her banking app and counts 11 monthly charges: streaming, music, cloud storage, a gym, a meal app, a news site, and a few she barely remembers.
She cancels three. None of them was bad. She liked two of them. They just lost a contest they didn't know they were in.

image.label: A phone showing a list of monthly charges, three crossed out
image.brief: 소파에 앉은 사람이 스마트폰으로 은행 앱을 보는 장면. 화면에 작은 월정액 결제 11줄이 나열되고 그중 세 줄에 빨간 줄이 그어져 있음. 실제 서비스 로고나 상표는 쓰지 말고 아이콘은 추상적인 도형으로.

cards.title: Your customers are doing their January cleanup.
body: You run a meditation app at $9 a month. Every January, cancellations jump as people review their spending. Reviews are good. People who cancel often say "I just wasn't using it enough."
What protects you most before next January?

options.text: Add lots of new content so the app feels worth more
options.feedback: More content raises value on paper. But people who already don't open the app won't notice it, so it rarely changes their ranking.

options.text: Cut the price to $6 so it's too small to bother cancelling
options.feedback: Cheaper helps a little, but you lose a third of revenue from everyone, including loyal users. A low-use $6 charge still looks cuttable.

options.text: Build a weekly habit and show users what they got each month
options.feedback: This moves you up the list people make in January. It costs effort in product and messaging, not price.

cards.title: The cleanup is a ranking, not a verdict.
body: When Maya reviewed her charges, she didn't ask "Is this service good?" She asked "Which of these could I live without?"
That question puts every subscription on one list. Each charge looked small alone. The **total** felt big. So she ranked them by how much she used and missed them, and cut from the bottom.
The cancelled services weren't beaten by rivals. They were beaten by her other subscriptions.

cards.title: Subscription fatigue
body: **Subscription fatigue** is the tiredness customers feel as recurring charges pile up. At some point it pushes them to review the whole list and cut.

The new way to see it: your subscription is judged next to every other charge on the same statement. Your real competitor is often not a similar product. It's anything else the customer pays for each month.

image.label: Recurring charges stacked and ranked, bottom ones fading out
image.brief: 정기 결제 카드들이 위에서 아래로 쌓인 탑 형태. 위쪽 카드는 진하고 선명, 아래로 갈수록 흐려지며 맨 아래 2~3장이 가위로 잘려 떨어짐. 왼쪽 축에 'Used often'에서 'Rarely used'로 가는 화살표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: What turns autopay back into a decision
body: A subscription is safe while it runs on autopilot. These moments wake the customer up:
list: **Seeing the total:** a bank statement, a budgeting app, year-end taxes
**A price increase notice:** it invites a fresh look
**A renewal reminder,** especially for a yearly charge
**Finding a forgotten charge,** which makes people check the rest
**A tighter budget:** a new baby, a move, a slow quarter
cards.callout: Each trigger asks the same question: would I sign up again today?

cards.title: Businesses hold cleanups too.
body: Companies collect recurring charges the same way: software tools, equipment service plans, cleaning contracts, delivery programs. Each was approved by someone, for a good reason, at a different time.

Then a finance team adds them up. The review looks just like Maya's Sunday night, with a spreadsheet instead of an app. Vendors that no one can explain clearly get cut or merged into a bigger contract.

cards.title: Fatigue isn't a reason to give up on subscriptions.
body: Customers keep the subscriptions they use often and would miss. Fatigue punishes low-use, easy-to-forget offers, not recurring revenue itself. Switching to one-time sales doesn't fix weak usage.
The tempting fix is to hide the cancel button or bury charges in vague names. That may delay one cancellation, but it makes the next review harsher and costs you trust when customers notice.

cards.title: Now it's a factory supplier.
body: You make replacement filters for dust-extraction machines and ship them to small workshops every quarter on auto-renewal. Each year, many owners and their accountants review every recurring vendor charge.
Renewal season is coming. What do you do?

options.text: Raise the price slightly before reviews start, while customers are still on autopilot
options.feedback: You gain a bit per order now. But a price increase is itself a trigger, and it lands right when customers are ranking vendors.

options.text: Send each workshop a yearly summary of filters shipped and downtime avoided, plus an easy way to change frequency
options.feedback: You give the reviewer a clear reason to keep you, and flexibility beats a full cancel. Some may ship less often, but you stay on the list.

options.text: Add gloves and masks to every shipment to make the plan look like better value
options.feedback: It may feel generous, but it raises the total on the statement. Customers who didn't ask for the extras now have more to question.

cards.softwareNote: The same yearly summary works for software: a renewal email showing hours saved or files stored gives the person reviewing the invoice a reason to keep it.

cards.title: Your subscription is judged next to every other one.
body: Customers don't cancel only bad services. They cancel whatever ranks lowest when they finally look at the total. Stay near the top by being used often and making the value easy to see.
**Try it today:** list your own recurring charges and rank them by use. Then ask where your product sits on your customers' lists.
